title: Factory legislation spreads to all trades
claim: Extension of factory legislation to all trades is inevitable, driven by the need to protect the working class; he sees an irresistible tendency toward its general application, including agriculture.
quote: an irresistible tendency towards the general application of those principles
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Can be checked against the spread of labour-protection law across sectors and countries.
notes: Agricultural attempts had so far 'resulted in complete failure' per Marx.

title: Factory regulation accelerates concentration of capital
claim: Regulating small workshops speeds the conversion of many small industries into a few large combined ones, so concentration of capital and the exclusive predominance of the factory system advance.
quote: accelerates the concentration of capital and the exclusive predominance of the factory system
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable against firm-size distributions and whether small-shop sectors consolidated after regulation.

title: Regulation destroys last safety-valve and matures contradictions
claim: By destroying petty and domestic industry, factory law removes the last resort of the redundant population (the safety-valve of the social mechanism), and by maturing material conditions provides the forces for exploding the old society while forming elements of the new.
quote: the forces for exploding the old one
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Implies heightened social antagonism/system rupture; checkable but with a vague timeline and partly dialectical wording.
notes: Revolutionary conclusion partly dialectical; the safety-valve claim is more specific than the explosion claim.

title: Regulation intensifies labour and spurs technical change
claim: Limiting the working day does not just constrain capital: it spurs technical improvement, raises intensity of labour and increases competition of machinery with the labourer, while raising order within each workshop and anarchy in capitalism as a whole.
quote: the immense spur which the limitation and regulation of the working day give
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable against productivity/intensity trends after hours limits.

title: Capitalist agriculture annihilates the peasantry
claim: Modern industry in agriculture annihilates the peasant, replaces him with the wage-labourer, evens out class antagonisms between country and town, and concentrates the population in cities (rural population falling absolutely).
quote: it annihilates the peasant, that bulwark of the old society
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Rural population, peasant share and farm wage-labour can be tracked, including counter-cases (family farms).
notes: Cites Cambridge/Suffolk rural depopulation; US machines only 'virtually' displacing labour so far.

title: Soil exhaustion and rift in the metabolism of man and earth
claim: Capitalist agriculture, concentrating population in towns, disrupts the circulation of matter between man and soil, violating the conditions of lasting fertility; every advance in capitalist agriculture robs the soil as well as the labourer, and the process is fastest in the most industrialised new countries such as the US.
quote: a progress towards ruining the lasting sources of that fertility
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Soil degradation, fertiliser dependence and nutrient cycling are measurable; counter-evidence (synthetic fertiliser) is also assessable.
notes: Relies on Liebig (fn. 246). Marx also says the process 'imperiously calls for' restoration as a systematic law of social production.

title: State oversight is evaded when enforcement is thin
claim: English factory/workshop/mines laws were largely dead letters because of tiny inspectorates, owner-dominated committees and workers' fear of victimisation; Parliament accepted regulation in principle yet resisted in practice. Mines: 12 inspectors for 3,217 mines in 1865, explosions growing.
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable against enforcement capacity and compliance over time, and against accident trends.
notes: Includes Select Committee evidence (source: miners, Times). Marx notes the 1872 Act as first limit on mine hours for children.

title: Absolute vs relative surplus-value and real subjection
claim: Absolute surplus-value turns on lengthening the working day; relative surplus-value revolutionises technical processes and the composition of society. Formal subjection of labour to capital is replaced in development by real subjection. Once capitalism is general, relative surplus-value is the method that continues to operate through revolutions in production.
quote: revolutionises out and out the technical processes of labour, and the composition of society
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Largely a definitional/analytic framework; hard to falsify as stated.

title: Mill: profit arises from durability and productivity of labour
claim: Mill says profit arises because labour produces more than its support and because capital goods outlast the time to produce them; profit would exist even without exchange or division of employments; profit rate equals the percentage by which labour exceeds wages. Marx calls this tautology and confusion of rate of surplus-value with rate of profit.
quote: The cause of profit is that labour produces more than is required for its support.
speaker: opponent:John Stuart Mill
testable_rationale: Theoretical dispute about the source of profit; Marx's refutation is arithmetic/definitional.
notes: Marx's rebuttal: 4% not 20% profit on £500 capital.

title: Rising productivity widens the abyss between worker and capitalist
claim: Even if the mass of necessaries a worker obtains grows, productivity gains that cheapen labour-power raise surplus-value, so the gap between worker and capitalist keeps widening; the price of labour-power can keep falling while real consumption rises.
quote: the abyss between the labourer's position and that of the capitalist would keep widening
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable via labour share of income/inequality over time while real wages rise.
notes: Marx separates real wages from relative position; this is a claim of relative, not absolute, deterioration.

title: Shorter working day tends to be followed by higher productivity and intensity
claim: Arguments against shortening the working day assume constant productivity and intensity, but in reality a change in productiveness and intensity precedes or immediately follows a shortening; intensity and productiveness make shorter days possible, and shortening raises intensity.
quote: The more the productiveness of labour increases, the more can the working day be shortened
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable against output per hour after hours reductions in historical episodes.
notes: Cites factory inspectors (source) on the Ten Hours Act.

title: Under capitalism the working day cannot shrink to necessary labour
claim: Surplus labour cannot vanish under capital (shrinking the working day to the necessary labour-time is utterly impossible under the capitalist regime); the working day could fall to necessary labour only after abolishing the capitalist form, and even then the necessary part would expand with standard of life and accumulation fund.
quote: a consummation utterly impossible under the régime of capital
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable as a claim that hours will not fall below the level that preserves surplus labour; the boundary is loosely specified.
notes: Strongly worded 'impossible', though he treats it as a conceptual limit.

title: Wage form conceals unpaid labour
claim: The wage appears as payment for all labour (price of labour), erasing the division between paid and unpaid labour; this mirror-image phenomenal form underlies juridical notions of liberty and the apologetics of vulgar economy. Slavery and corvee show the division openly; wage labour hides it.
quote: The wage form thus extinguishes every trace of the division of the working day
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: An interpretive claim about ideology and appearance with no clear outcome that would contradict it.

title: Hourly and casual pay lets capital lengthen hours and cut regularity
claim: If wages are fixed per hour with no guaranteed hours, the link between paid and unpaid labour is destroyed: the capitalist can extort surplus labour without allowing necessary labour-time, make overwork alternate with idleness, and abnormally lengthen the day; legal limits end this but not machine competition and crises.
quote: He can annihilate all regularity of employment
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable against on-call/zero-hours and underemployment trends in hourly-pay regimes.
notes: Cites the 1860 London building trades revolt against hourly wage.

title: Long hours and low wages go together; overtime premium traps workers
claim: Where hours are long, wages per hour are low; low hourly pay compels workers into overtime to secure a living, and a normal day is treated as a fraction of the actual one; falling price of labour stimulates longer hours.
quote: the longer the working days, in any branch of industry, the lower are the wages
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Cross-sectional correlation of hours and hourly pay can be tested.
notes: Cites Redgrave, factory inspector (source).

title: Piece-wages promote intensity, subcontracting and falling average wages
claim: Piece-wage gives capital a measure of intensity, makes supervision superfluous, underlies domestic outwork and sub-letting ('sweating'), exploitation of labourer by labourer, and, by fostering individual competition, tends to lower the average wage while raising individual wages; it becomes the general rule under factory limits.
quote: a tendency, while raising individual wages above the average, to lower this average itself
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable against evidence on piece-rate/performance pay, gig subcontracting and average wage trends.
notes: Marx calls piece-wage 'the form of wages most in harmony with the capitalist mode of production'.

title: Employers: productivity gains of labour do not concern workers
claim: Capitalists/apologists (Bright & Co., 'On Combination of Trades') say workmen have no claim to share profits from new machinery and that demanding higher wages as labour is abbreviated is a tax on improvement; Watts says piece-workers are their own masters. Marx treats these as apologetic.
speaker: opponent:Watts / employers
testable_rationale: The factual question of whether productivity gains pass to wages is testable.
notes: Marx quotes the Bright & Co. case (source) as an illustration.

title: National differences of wages and the international law of value
claim: Countries with more developed capitalism have higher national intensity and productivity, hence higher nominal wages, but the relative price of labour (per unit product, vs surplus-value) can be lower; high nominal wages do not prove high real wages or high labour cost.
quote: the national intensity and productivity of labour there rise above the international level
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Compare unit labour costs vs wage levels across countries.
notes: Supported by factory inspector Redgrave (source) on spindles per operative; cites Cowell.

title: Reproduction of the capital relation
claim: Continuity of production reproduces not only goods and surplus-value but the capital relation itself: capitalist on one side, wage labourer on the other; the worker is bound by invisible threads, belongs to capital before selling himself, and wages are the worker's own prior product.
quote: the wage labourer is bound to his owner by invisible threads
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Structural/analytic claim; compatible with almost any distribution outcome.

title: Every capital becomes capitalised unpaid labour
claim: Even if capital originally came from the owner's own labour, simple reproduction eventually converts every capital into capitalised surplus-value; the older capital is consumed and what remains represents appropriated unpaid labour.
quote: sooner or later, and of necessity, converts every capital into accumulated capital, or capitalised surplus-value
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: An accounting/labour-theory claim about the origin of capital value, not independently falsifiable.
notes: Contrast with the political-economy story of 'primitive labour' and abstinence (ch24-p012, p029).

title: Capital treats worker consumption as productive only if it reproduces labour-power
claim: The capitalist and economist count as productive only the worker's consumption needed to perpetuate the class; capital seeks to reduce individual consumption to the strictly necessary and trusts the worker's instincts of self-preservation and propagation; rising wages with no extra demand for labour would be 'unproductive'.
quote: reduce the labourer's individual consumption as far as possible to what is strictly necessary
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable via wage share/consumption policy; but Marx hedges 'within the limits of what is strictly necessary'.
notes: Ricardo/Malthus/J. Mill in footnotes hold the 'productive consumption' view.

title: Capital claims proprietary right over a skilled labouring class
claim: In the cotton famine capitalists (Potter) treated skilled workers as the manufacturers' 'living machinery', opposed emigration, and public opinion kept the operatives locked in the cotton districts; the Times replied that human machinery rusts and spreads discontent. Skill accumulates across generations.
quote: they are the mental and trained power
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Compare how employers and states handle labour supply, migration and retraining in downturns.
notes: Potter's claims are from a source (a manufacturer's letter to the Times); the Times article is reported as a jeu d'esprit.

title: Accumulation is self-reinforcing
claim: The more the capitalist has accumulated, the more is he able to accumulate; ownership of past unpaid labour becomes the sole condition for appropriating living unpaid labour on a constantly increasing scale; capital arises from the unpaid labour of the working class (the tribute exacted by the capitalist class), and new capital may be a machine that replaces the producers with children.
quote: The more the capitalist has accumulated, the more is he able to accumulate.
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable as increasing concentration of wealth/capital with cumulative returns; compare wealth-inequality data.
notes: The machine-replaces-producers line anticipates later chapters on accumulation and the reserve army.

title: Laws of property turn into laws of capitalist appropriation
claim: Exchange of equivalents, applied consistently, produces appropriation without equivalent: each act of purchase of labour-power follows commodity-exchange law, yet the ensemble means that capital exchanged for labour-power is itself the product of others' unpaid labour. Capitalist appropriation arises from application, not violation, of commodity-production's property laws.
quote: changed into their very opposite
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: A dialectical/analytic claim ('inner dialectic') with no definite empirical prediction.
notes: The passage ch24-p017 to p035 is a later addition from the 4th German edition.

title: Social wealth becomes ever more the property of those who appropriate unpaid labour
claim: In the period of capitalism social wealth becomes to an ever-increasing degree the property of those in a position to appropriate unpaid labour of others continually, and original capital becomes a vanishing quantity relative to accumulated surplus-value.
quote: to an ever-increasing degree the property of those who are in a position to appropriate
speaker: marx
testable_rationale: Testable against the trend in concentration of wealth and capital's share, and against the proportion of capital that is accumulated profit.
notes: Related claim in the Economist quoted in fn. 11 (source).
